transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/time: 2027-01-15 14:00 PST (22:00Z)
- Duration: 70 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Lena Park (Orchid ML), Rajiv Menon (Orchid Staff ML Eng), Tom Baker (Orchid Infra)

Summary:
Quick, fairly deep tracewalk to understand a reproducible tail-latency spike Orchid saw on mixed GPU cluster: TRT-LLM path intermittently slower than vLLM path for long sequences, and CUDA graph replay occasionally causes kernel ordering diffs that evict KV cache. Goal: identify root cause (kernel selection, cudagraph replay nondeterminism, NVLink contention, or quantization codepath) and agree next steps to reproduce on Redwood Dedicated trial.

Topics:
- Kernel selection heuristics (TRT-LLM vs vLLM)
- CUDA graph capture / replay determinism and eviction behavior
- KV cache prefetch/eviction interactions with batching
- Quantization path differences (int8 vs 4-bit) and kernel fusion impact
- VPC / on-prem constraints for trace collection and Dedicated pilot

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. um quick intro, i'm maya, AE on the Redwood Dedicated trial team, and diego's gonna walk through the traces we collected.
[00:12] Lena Park: hi, yeah thanks. we saw a couple of tricky things in prod last week, we're trying to pin if it's cudagraph replay or something with nvlink in the hetero pool.
[00:20] Diego Alvarez: cool, so i'll share my screen of the tracewalk — i've got nvprof, Nsight and our micro flamegraphs. heads-up, some of the labels are fuzzy, the trace tool mislabels TRT nodes as TrtL, etc.
[00:35] Rajiv Menon: one quick data point — our workload is a multi-turn chat, average length ~600 tokens but tail to 2k tokens on heavy sessions. we batch at the ingress with dynamic batching that tries to keep latency under 200 ms p95.
[00:51] Tom Baker: infra side, this is a heterogeneous farm — A100 + H100 mixed, NVLink between subset, PCIe elsewhere, and we do multi-tenant packing.
[01:07] Diego Alvarez: ok first slide, kernel timeline. notice at ~t=12s the TensorRT path chooses fused attention kernel variant A_v2, while vLLM path uses cuBLAS-mm + custom attention; on some runs the fused kernel has higher mem temp usage and triggers eviction of older KV pages.
[01:30] Rajiv Menon: do you mean eviction from device DRAM or our persistent KV cache? because we've seen the KV cache TTL get reset when cudagraph replay happens.
[01:39] Diego Alvarez: yeah both — there appears to be subtle ordering diffs in cudagraph replay where the capture doesn't include a short prefetch, so the replay inserts a different memory pressure footprint, which can lead the runtime to spill older KV blocks.
[01:54] Lena Park: that matches what we saw where the next prompt after a long session had a cold start and latency spiked.
[02:03] Maya Chen: can you explain why cudagraph replay would change ordering? isn't it supposed to be deterministic?
[02:10] Diego Alvarez: in theory yes, but practical caveats: 1) CUDA graph capture can fold some ephemeral exchanges; 2) if code path selection differs between capture and replay (ex: quantized kernel chosen at replay because of different dtype alignment), the graph nodes map to different kernel implementations; 3) small runtime optimizations (kernel fusion) can change launch grouping. all of these can change the memory working set transiently.
[02:36] Tom Baker: we do have mixed-precision fallback for a subset of models — sometimes the int8 path fails and it falls back to int16, could that flip kernel selection?
[02:44] Diego Alvarez: absolutely. the quant path can change the kernel selector table entries — TRT prefers fused kernels for int8/4bit, whereas vLLM tends to go with separate attention + GEMM kernels that have different memory footprints.
[03:00] Rajiv Menon: is there a way to force consistent kernel selection across capture and replay?
[03:07] Diego Alvarez: yes a few levers: set explicit kernel preference config in the runtime (we can pin to 'fused-off' or 'fused-prefer'), and ensure the capture input dtypes and sequence lengths match the replay. also deterministic CUDA stream ordering helps — we saw fights when multiple streams interleave.
[03:26] Lena Park: we do use multiple compute streams for packing. could that interleaving affect cudagraph?
[03:32] Diego Alvarez: if capture spans operations across streams, the graph capture model might serialize them differently on replay — which can reorder memory allocation lifetimes. that's likely why your KV pages were evicted.
[03:45] Maya Chen: ok sounds like we should reproduce with single stream capture and forced kernel pins. next, can you show the flamegraphs?
[03:52] Diego Alvarez: sure. (screen) here's two runs side by side. run A is TRT-LLM path with 4-bit quant; run B is vLLM-like path with 16-bit. You can see the TRT run has a large spike in attention-mma kernel runtime at t~9s, but also a larger transient mem alloc region.
[04:15] Rajiv Menon: interesting, so even though TRT had a faster median, its tail is worse. we've also seen this when NVLink congestion occurs.
[04:23] Diego Alvarez: NVLink shows up in the trace as queued host->device memcpy times — when we hit a cross-node KV fetch it can add hundreds of ms and exacerbate kernel ordering side-effects.
[04:33] Tom Baker: on our topology a KV miss can go across NVLink to a remote GPU. sometimes that route is congested with other tenants.
[04:42] Diego Alvarez: that's a good point — multi-tenant packing + cross-node KV fetch is a compounding factor. Redwood's smart routing can prefer local replica for latency SLOs; for Dedicated trial we can reserve NVLink-only placement for your model to avoid cross-host fetches.
[04:58] Lena Park: what's involved in that reservation? is that Dedicated-only?
[05:03] Maya Chen: yes, placement pins are a Dedicated feature — we can set node-affinity for model shards and routing rules in the console. we'll include the config snippet in the follow-up.
[05:11] Rajiv Menon: back to cudagraph nondeterminism — is there a way to log the exact kernel implementations chosen so we can correlate with eviction events?
[05:20] Diego Alvarez: we added a trace flag that dumps kernel selector table per-capture and per-replay. i'll attach that. it outputs kernel hashes, implementation names (imperfect), and memory footprint estimates.
[05:30] Tom Baker: great. any pointers on how to capture this in our VPC/on-prem setup? we don't want to leak internal IPs when we share traces.
[05:38] Diego Alvarez: for security we recommend redacting IPs and using the on-prem collection agent — it produces a sanitized trace file that strips host names, and we can set up a short-lived S3 presigned upload into Redwood's private bucket. we'll send the onboarding doc.
[05:52] Lena Park: perfect. another question: quantization — we've tried both 8-bit and 4-bit QAT; do you observe different kernel fusion behavior?
[06:01] Diego Alvarez: yes, 4-bit tends to use packed GEMM kernels which are more likely to be fused into attention kernels in TRT. that fusion reduces kernel count but increases per-kernel memory working set because of temporary buffers for packing/unpacking. result: lower token cost but potentially higher transient peak memory and tail latency.
[06:20] Rajiv Menon: so it's a cost vs tail-latency tradeoff. could we run mixed modes — e.g., int8 for shorter sequences and 16-bit for long sessions?
[06:29] Maya Chen: Redwood Optimize has workload signals to suggest a quantization split. we can do runtime routing so long sessions go to a 'robust' model variant. Diego, we talked about auto-fallback earlier?
[06:40] Diego Alvarez: yes, Redwood runtime supports model variant routing by sequence length or token budget. we can also set grace periods so cache warms on variant switch. problem is when cudagraph replay happens with one variant and replay chooses another, you get mismatched traces. hence the need to keep capture/replay variant pinned.
[06:58] Tom Baker: how reproducible is the nondeterministic cudagraph behavior? we saw it maybe 1 in 20 runs.
[07:05] Diego Alvarez: small differences in memory allocator free lists and timing can flip it. it's inherently racy in multi-stream and multi-tenant contexts but we can make it rarer by: single-stream capture for reproductions, pinning kernel selector tables, and disabling ephemeral allocators during capture.
[07:23] Lena Park: for our next step we'll run Diego's capture with these pins and report back.
[07:30] Maya Chen: great. want to talk briefly about Dedicated pilot logistics?
[07:35] Lena Park: yes please. what's the minimal footprint to reproduce?
[07:39] Diego Alvarez: for your NVLink case, 2 H100s in same NVLink domain is minimum. we can provide a small Dedicated pool with 2 NVLink-connected instances for two weeks. that should surface the cross-node KV behavior.
[07:53] Rajiv Menon: cost-wise, how do pilots work?
[07:56] Maya Chen: i'll send options — we have credit-backed trial and discounted pilot pricing for PoCs. i'll include the SKU for NVLink-connected nodes and an onboarding checklist.
[08:05] Tom Baker: last security thing — we'll need KMS integration for keys and an audit trail. what's Redwood's support there?
[08:12] Maya Chen: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit log exports. for Dedicated we offer integration points to your KMS via IAM roles; Diego can link the specific docs.
[08:23] Diego Alvarez: i'll add that to the doc bundle.
[08:27] Lena Park: ok quick recap?
[08:30] Maya Chen: recap — Diego will share tracewalk scripts and kernel selector dumps; Orchid runs pinned single-stream capture with kernel pins and runs NVLink 2-node benchmark; Redwood provisions a 2-week Dedicated NVLink pool; Maya sends pricing and security docs.
[08:45] Rajiv Menon: sounds right. thanks everyone.
[08:49] Tom Baker: thanks.
[08:50] Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links to the shared folder and an initial timeline.
